cues.text: Blood in the Washing
In 1294, a young housemaid of the church rectory in Gruaro , a small town in the Veneto, carried an altar cloth from the Church of St. Giusto.
She took it to the public washhouse of the Versiola stream to launder it as she did any other day.
As she worked the linen through the water, she noticed a consecrated Host had been left, apparently by mistake, folded among its creases — and that blood was flowing from it into the cloth around it.
A Bishop Confirms the Sign
Frightened by what she had found, the young woman ran at once to inform the parish priest.
He organized a solemn procession to carry the stained cloth and recovered Host back to the church.
He then reported the matter to the Bishop of Concordia, Giacomo d'Ottonello of Cividale , who examined the account and confirmed the sign as genuine.
A Relic Two Towns Both Wanted
The bishop initially asked that the cloth be brought to his own cathedral at Concordia.
However, the parish of Gruaro and the noble family of the Counts of Valvasone each wished to keep the relic for their own.
The family were patrons of the churches in both towns; unable to reach agreement, the dispute was ultimately referred to the Holy See.
A Sanctuary at Valvasone
Rome allowed the Counts of Valvasone to keep the relic on the condition that they build a proper church to house it.
Construction of the Church of the Most Holy Body of Christ at Valvasone was completed in 1483, nearly two centuries after the miracle itself.
The oldest surviving document describing the event in detail is a decree of Pope Nicholas V from 1454.
Legacy
The relic remains enshrined today at Valvasone, several miles from Gruaro, where a monument still marks the presumed site of the original miracle along the banks of the Versiola.
Every Corpus Christi, the community renews a devotion now more than seven centuries old.
This proves that even a dispute between two towns and two noble houses could not, in the end, keep so small a sign from finding a lasting home.
